parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Dust and the American West
parts.article:
Dust and the American West
 
(A) Images of deserts in the United States show dusty, barren landscapes, but the land may not always have been this way. Ever since settlers moved west across the US, there has been dust, clouds of it, everywhere. It was part of the landscape, or so it seemed to them. But there were no records of the landscape of the West until the settlers arrived. Now, evidence is starting to emerge which suggests that before the settlers, there was very little dust. The evidence comes from the San Juan Mountains of southwest Colorado, downwind of Arizona and New Mexico. There, Jason Neff, a geochemist from the University of Colorado, has been analyzing sediments, the sand, stones and mud, laid down over the past 5,000 years. Atmospheric dust was minimal throughout those five millennia until the mid-19th century, he says, but then, 'from about 1860 to 1900, dust deposition rates shot up.'
 
(B) This is surprising because usually dry means dusty, and the American West has almost always been dry, often drier than today. There was a near-permanent drought between 900 and 1300 which was so intense that it destroyed a series of Native American civilizations, including the Anasazi, whose cliff homes are now US national treasures. Yet the evidence from the San Juan lakes is that it was not dusty. Even as their civilization was collapsing, the Anasazi seem to have protected their soils from erosion.
 
(C) This was not the case with the European settlers once they brought their cows. The landscape the cattle were introduced to was remarkably ill-equipped to cope with grazing animals, says Neff. 'Unlike most other parts of the US, there were few grazers in the American Southwest until the Europeans came. No bison and few antelope or deer.'
 
(D) In the Great Plains to the east and north, bison roamed in vast herds. Their regular grazing had created tough grass, while the herds manured the soil. In the Southwest, the land had few defenses against a sudden invasion of millions of livestock, whose teeth stripped the grass and whose hooves punctured the hard crust of desert soils that protected them from the wind. The invasion was sudden, funded by a bubble of speculative investment, much of it from Britain. The money went into railroads and herds of cattle and sheep that rode the rails to the wide open pastures. By 1900, when sedimentation rates peaked, there were 20 million cattle and 25 million sheep in the West.
 
(E) One of the biggest ranches was owned by the Aztec Land and Cattle Company, which owned a million acres of land by 1884. Each acre had cost the company a mere 50 cents, and like many other speculators, it was only interested in quick profits and had little incentive to protect the soils from overgrazing. By the time Aztec sold the ranch in 1901, it was barren, with cattle carcasses scattered across the exhausted land. Such was the damage to the grasslands that even now few of the pastures have recovered. The parched and exposed soil simply blew away. The 1862 Homestead Act was passed in order to encourage the populating of the West. Any family willing to make the journey was entitled to claim 160 acres and farm it. Yet by the time people moved west in large numbers, the cattle companies had taken most of the land and surrounded it with barbed wire. The water sources were therefore cut off, and were aggressively guarded. It was only in the 1930s, with the passage of the Taylor Grazing Act, that federal authorities finally sought to limit cattle herds.
 
(F) Soil scientists have known for a while about the importance of the hard crust that forms on arid soils. 'These crusts can survive winds of up to a hundred miles an hour, but cattle hooves break the crust,' says Jayne Belnap, a soil ecologist at the US Geological Survey, Utah. The scale of the dust clouds created by the livestock invasion has until now been largely unknown. When Neff first discovered dust in Colorado lake sediments laid down in the 19th century, he was initially unsure where it came from. Maybe it had crossed the Pacific from China's Gobi Desert.
 
(G) But after investigating the size and chemical composition of the dust, Neff was clear that it mostly came from the American Southwest, mainly Arizona and New Mexico. Now, with the soil crusts gone, dust clouds still head north and are having significant ecological effects in the Colorado mountains. They carry nutrients with them into areas which previously evolved and survived without them. But perhaps the most dramatic impact of the dust has been on snowfields in the Rocky Mountain Range. Even a thin sprinkling of dark material means snow absorbs more solar radiation, meaning that snowmelt occurs far more rapidly during springtime. The impact on the ski tourism industry is obvious.
 
(H) The loss of snow and the shrinking of glaciers across the American West in the past century have been dramatic. Glacier National Park in Montana, for example, has lost three quarters of its snow cover since 1910. All this is frequently attributed to global warming. While this almost certainly plays a role, Neff's findings suggest that dust may also contribute.

questions.question: Jason Neff discovered there had been a dramatic rise in dust levels in the second half of the nineteenth century.

analyses.content: “Shot up” 是 “dramatic rise” 的生动表达，时间段 1860-1900 完全吻合 19世纪下半叶。
(Paragraph A) “...but then, 'from about 1860 to 1900, dust deposition rates shot up.'”
题目说Jason Neff发现19世纪下半叶沙尘水平急剧上升。原文A段末尾提到“从大约1860年到1900年（即19世纪下半叶），沙尘沉积率猛增（shot up）”，选 TRUE。

questions.question: The Anasazi civilization disappeared due to the impact of dust in the atmosphere.

analyses.content: 题目说阿纳萨齐文明因大气中沙尘的影响而消失。原文B段确实提到了他们的消失，但原因是大旱（drought），且明确指出当时“was not dusty（没有沙尘）”，选 FALSE。
题目把因果关系搞错了，原文说导致文明毁灭的是干旱，而且特意强调那时候反而没有沙尘（因为他们保护了土壤）。
(Paragraph B) “There was a near-permanent drought... that it destroyed a series of Native American civilizations... Yet the evidence... is that it was not dusty.”

questions.question: Before cattle were introduced to the American Southwest, large numbers of bison occupied the area.

analyses.content: 题目说在牛被引入美国西南部之前，该地区有大量野牛（bison）。原文C段明确说在欧洲人到来之前，美国西南部“No bison（没有野牛）”，选 FALSE。
必须看清地点是“American Southwest”，原文对比了其他地方，指出这里“Unlike most other parts... No bison”。
(Paragraph C) “'Unlike most other parts of the US, there were few grazers in the American Southwest until the Europeans came. No bison and few antelope or deer.'”

questions.question: The bison population in the Great Plains diminished because European settlers found it easy to hunt them.

analyses.content: 不要利用常识（虽然历史上确实是被猎杀的），文中没有这句话，雅思阅读只看文章给出的信息。
题目说大平原的野牛数量减少是因为欧洲定居者发现很容易猎杀它们。原文D段虽然提到了大平原的野牛（bison roamed in vast herds），但完全没有提及它们数量减少的原因或是否容易被猎杀，选 NOT GIVEN。
(Paragraph D) “In the Great Plains to the east and north, bison roamed in vast herds.” (仅此而已，无下文关于猎杀的描述)

questions.question: The development of railroads across the US was more expensive than originally expected.

analyses.content: 题目说美国铁路建设的成本超出了最初的预期。原文D段只提到资金流入了铁路和牛群（money went into railroads），并没有比较“实际成本”和“预期成本”，选 NOT GIVEN。
文中提到了“speculative investment（投机投资）”和“money”，但没提到是否超支。
(Paragraph D) “The invasion was sudden, funded by a bubble of speculative investment... The money went into railroads...”

questions.question: The Aztec Land and Cattle Company worked hard to take care of the grazing land it owned.

analyses.content: 题目说Aztec土地和养牛公司努力照顾其拥有的牧场。原文E段说该公司只对快速获利感兴趣，“had little incentive to protect the soils（几乎没有动力去保护土壤）”，选 FALSE。
“Little incentive to protect” 直接反驳了 “worked hard to take care”。
(Paragraph E) “...it was only interested in quick profits and had little incentive to protect the soils from overgrazing.”

questions.question: Most of the land once owned by the Aztec Land and Cattle Company remains infertile today.

analyses.content: (Paragraph E) “Such was the damage to the grasslands that even now few of the pastures have recovered.”
“Few have recovered” 等同于 “Most remain infertile”。
题目说Aztec公司曾经拥有的土地大部分今天仍然贫瘠。原文E段说对草地的破坏如此严重，以至于“even now few of the pastures have recovered（即使到现在也没几个牧场恢复了）”，即大部分仍未恢复/贫瘠，选 TRUE。

analyses.content: 题目说1930年代通过法律来控制____的规模，原文E段末尾提到随着泰勒放牧法的通过，联邦当局终于寻求限制“cattle herds（牛群）”，填 cattle herds。
“Control the size of” 对应原文的 “limit”。
(Paragraph E) “It was only in the 1930s... federal authorities finally sought to limit cattle herds.”
题目说Jayne Belnap认为土壤未受到强____的影响，原文F段引用她说这些地壳可以经受高达每小时100英里的“winds（风）”幸存下来，即不受影响，填 winds。
“Not affected by” 对应 “survive”，“high” 对应 “up to a hundred miles an hour”。
(Paragraph F) “'These crusts can survive winds of up to a hundred miles an hour...”
(Paragraph F) “When Neff first discovered dust in Colorado lake sediments laid down in the 19th century...”
题目说Neff发现科罗拉多地区的____含有沙尘，原文F段提到Neff首次在科罗拉多“lake sediments（湖泊沉积物）”中发现沙尘，填 lake sediments。
题目是介词 in，原文是 discovered dust in...，直接锁定位置名词。
题目说检查了沙尘的化学成分以及____，原文G段开头说在调查了沙尘的“size（大小）”和化学成分之后，填 size。
并列连词 “and” 连接了 size 和 chemical composition，题目中是 as well as，结构一致。
(Paragraph G) “But after investigating the size and chemical composition of the dust...”
题目说沙尘通过带入通常不在那里的____来影响山区环境，原文G段说它们把“nutrients（营养物质）”带入那些以前没有它们也进化和生存的地区，填 nutrients。
“Not normally found there” 对应 “survived without them”。
(Paragraph G) “They carry nutrients with them into areas which previously evolved and survived without them.”
题目说沙尘部分导致了一些____和雪的逐渐消失，原文H段第一句提到过去一个世纪美国西部雪的流失和“glaciers（冰川）”的萎缩，填 glaciers。
题目是 “disappearance of some ______ and snow”，原文是 “loss of snow and the shrinking of glaciers”。
(Paragraph H) “The loss of snow and the shrinking of glaciers across the American West... Neff's findings suggest that dust may also contribute.”
